title: Ensemble Methods Deep Dive
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Ensemble Methods Deep Dive ##### The stack that was worse than its best member A team in Bengaluru built a stacking ensemble for demand forecasting. Five base models — Ridge, Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost — feeding a linear meta-learner. Cross-validated RMSE of the stack: 218. Best single model, LightGBM: 211. The ensemble was worse than one of its own members, which surprised them. The diagnosis took one line: ```python print(oof_predictions.corr()) ``` The three gradient boosting models correlated at 0.987, 0.991 and 0.989 with each other. Ridge correlated at 0.94 with the rest. Effectively they had four copies of the same model, and averaging four copies of a thing gives you the thing — plus the meta-learner's own estimation noise. Replacing two of the boosters with a k-NN model and a neural network — both substantially worse individually, both making *different* errors — dropped the stack to 194. **Ensembles work through diversity, not through model count.** That is the entire subject, and it is the part most tutorials skip. ##### The bias-variance view Total expected error decomposes into three parts: ``` E[(y − ŷ)²] = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise ``` **Bias** is systematic error from wrong assumptions — a straight line fitted to curved data. **Variance** is sensitivity to the particular training sample — a deep tree that restructures when you change ten rows. Ensembles attack these separately, and knowing which one you have determines which ensemble to build. For N models with individual variance σ² and average pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is: ``` Var(average) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/N ``` That formula is the whole story. As N grows, the second term vanishes — but **the first term does not**. It is floored at `ρσ²`. ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt sigma2 = 1.0 N = np.arange(1, 101) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) for rho in [0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 0.99]: var = rho * sigma2 + (1 - rho) * sigma2 / N ax.plot(N, var, label=f"ρ = {rho}") ax.set_xlabel("number of models"); ax.set_ylabel("variance of the average") ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Correlation floors the benefit of ensembling") ``` At ρ = 0.99 — the Bengaluru situation — a hundred models reduce variance by 1%. At ρ = 0.3, ten models get you most of the available benefit. **Diversity is not a nice-to-have. It is the mechanism.** | Family | Base learners | Trained | Reduces | Overfits with more models? | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Bagging** | Deep, low-bias, high-variance | Parallel, independent | Variance | No | | **Boosting** | Shallow, high-bias, low-variance | Sequential, dependent | Bias | **Yes** | | **Stacking** | Diverse types | Parallel, then a meta-learner | Both | Mildly | | **Voting** | Diverse types | Parallel | Variance | No | ##### Bagging and Random Forests Bagging creates diversity through **bootstrap sampling** — each model trains on a different random sample drawn with replacement, containing about 63.2% of the unique original rows. Random Forest adds a second, more important source: **at every split, only a random subset of features is considered.** Why that second source matters more than it sounds. Without it, if one feature is strongly predictive, every tree splits on it first and all 500 trees look nearly identical — ρ approaches 1 and the variance formula tells you averaging gains nothing. Forcing each split to choose from `√p` random features compels some trees to find alternative signals. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, ExtraTreesRegressor from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold import pandas as pd cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) for max_features in [1.0, 0.6, "sqrt", "log2"]: rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=max_features, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1) scores = -cross_val_score(rf, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") rf.fit(X_train, y_train) # Measure the diversity directly tree_preds = np.array([t.predict(X_val.values) for t in rf.estimators_]) avg_corr = np.corrcoef(tree_preds).mean() print(f"max_features={str(max_features):6s} RMSE {scores.mean():7.2f} " f"mean tree correlation {avg_corr:.3f}") ``` Run that and you see the trade directly: lower `max_features` gives lower tree correlation and, up to a point, better ensemble performance — even though each individual tree is worse. `ExtraTreesRegressor` pushes further by randomising the split **threshold** as well as the feature. More diversity, faster to train, individually weaker trees, and often a better ensemble. **Out-of-bag scoring** is a free validation estimate that comes with bagging. Each tree omits ~36.8% of rows; averaging predictions from only the trees that did not see a given row gives an unbiased estimate with no separate holdout: ```python rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, oob_score=True, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"OOB R²: {rf.oob_score_:.4f}") print(f"CV R²: {cross_val_score(rf, X_train, y_train, cv=cv).mean():.4f}") ``` Those two numbers should agree closely, which is a useful sanity check on your CV setup. **Adding trees to a Random Forest never overfits.** Performance plateaus, typically around 200–500, and more trees only cost time. This is a genuine difference from boosting and worth internalising. ##### Boosting Boosting builds models **sequentially**, each fitted to the errors of everything built so far. ``` F₀(x) = a constant (the mean for regression, log-odds for classification) for m in 1..M: residuals rᵢ = −∂L(yᵢ, F(xᵢ)) / ∂F(xᵢ) the negative gradient fit a shallow tree hₘ to those residuals Fₘ(x) = Fₘ₋₁(x) + η · hₘ(x) η = learning rate (shrinkage) ``` For squared error the gradient *is* the residual, which is where the intuition "each tree fits what the last one got wrong" comes from. The general form works for any differentiable loss. ```python from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor class TinyBoosting: def __init__(self, n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3): self.n, self.lr, self.depth = n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth def fit(self, X, y): self.init_ = y.mean() pred = np.full(len(y), self.init_) self.trees = [] for _ in range(self.n): residual = y - pred # what remains wrong tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=self.depth).fit(X, residual) pred += self.lr * tree.predict(X) # small step self.trees.append(tree) return self def predict(self, X): pred = np.full(len(X), self.init_) for t in self.trees: pred += self.lr * t.predict(X) return pred ``` Each tree is a **weak learner** — depth 3 is barely a model alone. Hundreds of them summed form a strong one, and the base learners are deliberately high-bias because boosting's job is to reduce bias. **Boosting overfits with more models**, unlike bagging. Early stopping is mandatory: ```python import lightgbm as lgb model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=5000, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=42, verbose=-1) model.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_train, y_train), (X_val, y_val)], eval_names=["train", "valid"], eval_metric="rmse", callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(150, verbose=False), lgb.log_evaluation(0)]) print(f"stopped at {model.best_iteration_} of 5000 trees") lgb.plot_metric(model, metric="rmse") ``` The learning curve tells the story: training error falls steadily toward zero while validation error falls, plateaus, then rises. The divergence point is where memorisation begins. **Bagging versus boosting, in the bias-variance frame** — which is what the assignment asks: Bagging trains **deep, unpruned** trees. Each has low bias and high variance. Averaging N of them leaves bias unchanged (the average of unbiased estimators is unbiased) while cutting variance by the formula above. So bagging reduces variance. Boosting trains **shallow** trees. Each has high bias and low variance. Summing them progressively reduces bias, because each new tree explicitly targets what the current ensemble gets wrong. Variance grows slowly as the ensemble becomes more complex, which is why it eventually overfits. ##### Voting The simplest ensemble: combine different model *types* and average. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import VotingRegressor, VotingClassifier from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler voter = VotingRegressor([ ("ridge", Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", RidgeCV())])), ("rf", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)), ("gbm", lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1)), ("knn", Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=15))])), ], weights=[1, 2, 3, 1]) ``` For classification, `voting="soft"` averages predicted probabilities and usually beats `"hard"` majority voting, because it uses the models' confidence rather than discarding it. **Model diversity comes from four sources**, and combining them multiplies the effect: - **Algorithm** — linear, tree, distance-based, neural. The strongest source. - **Features** — different subsets or different engineered representations. - **Data** — different bootstrap samples or time windows. - **Hyperparameters** — the same algorithm at very different settings. The weakest source. The Bengaluru stack varied only the fourth, which is why it failed. ##### Stacking Stacking (Wolpert, 1992) replaces the fixed averaging weights with a **learned** meta-model that discovers how to combine base predictions — including learning that one model is better in some regions of feature space and another elsewhere. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Training data] --> B1[Base model 1: Ridge] A --> B2[Base model 2: Random Forest] A --> B3[Base model 3: LightGBM] A --> B4[Base model 4: k-NN] B1 --> C[Out-of-fold predictions
from EACH base model] B2 --> C B3 --> C B4 --> C C --> D[Meta-learner trained on OOF predictions] D --> E[Final prediction] F[New data] --> G[Base models refit on ALL training data] G --> D ``` The critical mechanism is **out-of-fold predictions**. If base models predicted on data they trained on, those predictions would be optimistically accurate and the meta-learner would learn to trust them far too much. OOF predictions simulate what the base models produce on genuinely unseen data. ```python from sklearn.ensemble import StackingRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import KFold stack = StackingRegressor( estimators=[ ("ridge", Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", RidgeCV())])), ("rf", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)), ("gbm", lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1)), ("knn", Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=15))])), ], final_estimator=RidgeCV(), # keep the meta-learner SIMPLE cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), passthrough=False, # True adds original features too n_jobs=-1, ) ``` Three design rules that determine whether stacking helps. **Keep the meta-learner simple.** Ridge or a shallow linear model. A complex meta-learner overfits the OOF predictions, which are few in number and highly correlated. This is the most common stacking mistake. **Use enough folds.** Five is standard; fewer means noisier OOF predictions. **Diversity in the base models is the whole game**, which is where the correlation check comes in. Building it manually gives you the diagnostic the Bengaluru team needed: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict base_models = { "ridge": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", RidgeCV())]), "rf": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1), "gbm": lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1), "knn": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("m", KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=15))]), } oof = pd.DataFrame({ name: cross_val_predict(m, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, n_jobs=-1) for name, m in base_models.items() }) # THE diagnostic — correlation of ERRORS, not of predictions errors = oof.sub(y_train.values, axis=0) print("Error correlation matrix:") print(errors.corr().round(3)) print("\nIndividual RMSE:") for name in oof: print(f" {name:8s} {np.sqrt(((oof[name] - y_train) ** 2).mean()):.2f}") meta = RidgeCV().fit(oof, y_train) print("\nMeta-learner weights:") print(pd.Series(meta.coef_, index=oof.columns).round(3)) print(f"stack RMSE: {np.sqrt(((meta.predict(oof) - y_train) ** 2).mean()):.2f}") ``` **Correlate the errors, not the predictions.** Two models both predicting a strong trend will have highly correlated *predictions* regardless of whether they are useful together — the errors are what tell you if they are making the same mistakes. Interpret the error correlation matrix directly: | Error correlation | Meaning | |---|---| | > 0.95 | Redundant. Drop one. | | 0.7 – 0.9 | Some benefit from combining | | 0.3 – 0.7 | **Good diversity** | | < 0.3 | Excellent, if both are individually decent | | Negative | Rare and extremely valuable | Negative meta-learner weights are informative rather than alarming — they mean the meta-learner is using one model to *correct* another's systematic bias. Constrain them to be non-negative only if you need interpretability. **Blending** is stacking's simpler cousin: instead of OOF predictions, hold out a single validation set, train base models on the rest, and train the meta-learner on that holdout. Faster, no fold leakage risk, and it wastes data. Use stacking unless training cost forces the shortcut. ##### Does it earn its cost? Ensembles bring real overhead: training time, serving latency, memory, and debugging difficulty. The honest evaluation: ```python import time from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate candidates = { "best single (LGBM)": base_models["gbm"], "voting": voter, "stacking": stack, } rows = [] for name, m in candidates.items(): t0 = time.perf_counter() res = cross_validate(m, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=1) rows.append({"model": name, "rmse": -res["test_score"].mean(), "std": res["test_score"].std(), "fit_seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}) print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)) ``` A stack that improves RMSE by 0.4% while taking 12× longer to train and requiring four models in production is usually the wrong choice. Ensembles are worth it when the metric improvement translates to real value — Kaggle leaderboards, fraud detection at scale, pricing — and not worth it for a dashboard refreshed weekly. ##### Common mistakes - Building an ensemble from four variants of the same algorithm. - Never checking error correlation between base models. - A complex meta-learner overfitting the OOF predictions. - Training the meta-learner on in-sample base predictions rather than OOF. - Adding trees to a boosted model without early stopping. - Expecting more trees to overfit a Random Forest (they do not). - Ignoring `max_features` in a forest, leaving trees highly correlated. - Reporting the stack's score without comparing to the best single model. - Deploying a five-model ensemble for a 0.3% improvement. - Using hard voting when soft voting is available. ##### Hands-on Build a stacking ensemble combining at least three genuinely diverse base models with a simple meta-learner. Before evaluating it, compute the out-of-fold error correlation matrix and predict which combinations will help. Then compare the stack against every base model individually and against simple voting, all on the same cross-validation splits. If the stack loses, diagnose why — the correlation matrix will tell you. For the mini-project, build an ensemble study implementing bagging, boosting, voting and stacking on the same dataset. Include the diversity analysis as a first-class section: error correlation heatmap, per-model performance, meta-learner weights, and the variance-reduction curve for different correlation levels. Deliberately construct one ensemble that fails through redundancy and one that succeeds through diversity, and explain the difference with your own numbers. Finish with a table of performance against training time and serving complexity, and a recommendation on whether the ensemble is worth deploying. For the assignment, explain using the bias-variance framework why bagging reduces variance while boosting reduces bias. Cover the depth of the base learners in each case, the variance formula and the role of ρ, and why one overfits with more models while the other does not. ##### Key takeaways - `Var(average) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/N` — correlation floors the benefit, so diversity is the mechanism, not model count. - Bagging uses deep high-variance learners trained in parallel; boosting uses shallow high-bias learners trained sequentially. - Random Forest's per-split feature sampling is what decorrelates the trees; without it, averaging gains little. - Stacking needs out-of-fold base predictions and a deliberately simple meta-learner. - Correlate the base models' *errors* before building anything, and compare the ensemble against your best single model.
practical_task_reference: Build a stacking ensemble that combines at least three diverse base models with a meta-learner, and compare its cross-validated performance to each base model and to simple voting.
mini_project_reference: Build an ensemble study on a dataset that implements bagging, boosting, voting, and stacking, analyzes the correlation of base-model errors, and explains why diversity did or didn't help.
assignment_reference: Explain, using the bias-variance framework, why bagging reduces variance while boosting reduces bias.
